newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch TV group Endemol sparkles on bourse debut.
newsitem.headline: Dutch TV group Endemol sparkles on bourse debut.

text.p: Dutch TV production company Endemol Entertainment made a sparkling debut on the Amsterdam bourse on Friday, quickly proving its mix of popular soap operas and quiz shows a winning formula.

Investors soon chased the shares to a high of 57.50 guilders, 9.50 guilders above the issue price set by global co-ordinator ABN AMRO. They quickly became the most active stock on an otherwise subdued bourse and by 1330 GMT more than six million shares had changed hands.
"Endemol should be in the portfolio of all institutional investors," said one dealer, adding that private investors also had a great appetite for the stock.

Within hours of the listing, a new competitor emerged on the scene when publishing company VNU moved into television production, announcing it would set up a joint venture with the UK's Chrysalis Group Plc.
The new joint venture said its sights were set on further expansion in Europe.
Analysts were generally upbeat on Endemol, saying further gains in the share price were likely, but defended the issue price and warned investors that the future may not be all plain sailing.
"The stock could rise to 60 guilders, but we should not forget that it's one with some risk involved," said analyst Johan van de Hoven at brokers NIB Strating.
Analysts said the company could face European regulatory hurdles in the future and that its strategy of establishing a foothold in foreign markets increased its risk factor.
Investors had clamoured for Endemol shares. According to ABN AMRO, the issue was 25 times oversubscribed, which forced it to close early on October 29 instead of the planned November 6.
The company was formed in 1994 through a merger of the TV production firms of joint chairmen Joop van den Ende and John de Mol and specialises in popular game shows, soaps and dramas.
Around 80 percent of its revenue comes from television production, with the rest from its live entertainment division.

A monthy ago Endemol issued bullish forecasts, saying it expected net profit to rise by 15 to 20 percent in the 1996/97 financial year from 60.5 million guilders in 1995/96. It also said sales and profits would double in five years.
It has an ambitious expansion and acquisition strategy, which is particularly focused on foreign markets.
Some 40 percent of the company's television programming turnover is generated outside the Netherlands, with some 30 percent coming from Germany alone.
Its main television operations outside the Nethlands include wholly-owned production subsidiaries in in Germany and Portugal as well as joint ventures in Spain and France.

Joint chairman De Mol said a month ago he viewed eastern Europe as a most promising growth market. He was optimisic about opportunities in Europe as the ending of state monopolies leads to the growth of independent TV channels looking to replace cheap U.S. shows with ones in their own language.
"We see growth of the television market in Europe because the market is maturing. There is a growing need for locally produced prime-time amusement," he said.
